response.query: Which estimators and diagnostics should we pre-specify to correct staggered-DiD/TWFE bias, detect heterogeneous effects, and triangulate with synthetic controls and IVs?
response.answer: Use two-way fixed effects (TWFE) and dynamic DID estimators to correct staggered-DiD bias, and triangulate with synthetic controls and IVs for heterogeneous effects.

results.content: In settings with more than two units and two time periods, the regression DiD model usually takes the following two-way ﬁxed eﬀect (TWFE) form: yit = αi + λt + δDDDit + ϵit, (2) where αi and λt are unit and time period ﬁxed eﬀects, which subsume the main eﬀects for Di and POSTt. Researchers commonly modify this TWFE model to include covariates, time trends, and dynamic treatment eﬀect estimation (e.g., by separately including indicators for the number of periods before or after the treatment).2 Notably, researchers apply the TWFE model to estimate δ in settings with staggered treatment timing. 3.1 Static Staggered DiD Estimates Goodman-Bacon (2021) shows that the “static” staggered DiD TWFE treatment eﬀect estimate (δDD of Eq., (2)) is a “weighted average of all possible two-group/two-period DiD estimators in the data.” For example, the TWFE estimate constitutes four possible 2x2s when there are three groups over the sample period (from from the earlierst period—t0—to the last period in the data—T): a never-treated group (denoted U), an earlier-treated group (denoted k) that is treated at time t∗ k, and a later-treated group (denoted l) that is treated at t∗ l .3 The ﬁrst two of the possible 2x2 DiD comparisons involve one treatment group (either the earlier- or the later-treated ﬁrms) and the untreated group (as control) over the whole sample window (from t0 to T). To the extent this occurs, these outcome trends are inappropriate counterfactuals for the later-treated units.4 Eq., (4) suggests the staggered DiD TWFE estimate can diﬀer from the sample-average ATT due to treatment eﬀect heterogeneity either over time or across groups, even when the parallel-trends assumption is satisﬁed (V WCT = 0). Sun and Abraham (2021) shows that the choice of exclusion periods could lead to biases in TWFE dynamic eﬀect estimates, particularly when researchers exclude post-treatment relative-time periods from event-study speciﬁcations. results.title: Synthetic difference-in-differences estimation with staggered treatment timing - ScienceDirect
results.content: I compare the estimators obtained using SynthDiD, TWFE, the group time average treatment effect estimator of Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021), and the partially pooled synthetic control method estimator of Ben-Michael et al. I find that in this staggered treatment setting, SynthDiD provides a numerically different estimate of the average treatment effect. To illustrate this estimator’s importance and distinction, I employ data from Abrams, 2012a, Abrams, 2012b to demonstrate the differences in estimators obtained through SynthDiD, a standard two-way fixed effects DiD estimator, the group-time average treatment effect estimator of Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021), and the partially pooled synthetic control method estimator of Ben-Michael et al. To demonstrate the use of the staggered-treatment timing synthetic difference-in-differences estimator, replication data from Abrams, 2012a, Abrams, 2012b are used to estimate the causal impact of a law adopted by different states in different years. This estimator, as extended to staggered treatment adoption settings in Porreca (2022), allows for a localized causal estimator in which treated units are compared to a never treated control group that is weighted on both the time and unit dimensions.

results.title: Synthetic Controls and Weighted Event Studies with Staggered Adoption
results.content: The synthetic control method aims to estimate treatment effects by constructing a weighted combination of control units, which represents what the treated group would have experienced in the absence of receiving the treatment. While DiD estimation assumes that the effects of unobserved confounders are constant over time, the synthetic control method allows for these effects to change over time, by re-weighting the control group so that it has similar pre-intervention characteristics to the treated group. Synthetic Control Methods for Comparative Case Studies: Estimating the Effect of California's Tobacco Control Program. Synthetic control methods are commonly applied in empirical research to estimate the effects of treatments or interventions on aggregate outcomes. The synthetic control method (SCM) is a popular approach for estimating the impact of a treatment on a single unit in panel data settings. In this paper we study estimation of and inference for average treatment effects in a setting with panel data. In this paper we develop new methods for estimating causal effects in settings with panel data, where a subset of units are exposed to a treatment during a subset of periods, and the goal is estimating counterfactual (untreated) outcomes for the treated unit/period combinations. In contrast, if there are few units and many periods, our proposed method approximates a synthetic control estimator where counterfactual outcomes are estimated through a regression of the lagged outcomes for the treated unit on lagged outcomes for the control units. Propensity score methods are widely used for estimating treatment effects from observational studies. A popular approach is to estimate propensity scores by maximum likelihood based on logistic regression, and then apply inverse probability weighted estimators or extensions to estimate treatment effects. The ability of matched sampling and linear regression adjustment to reduce the bias of an estimate of the treatment effect in two sample observational studies is investigated for a simple matching method and five simple estimates. In this paper an extension of this methodology is proposed that allows for estimation of average causal effects with multi-valued treatments while maintaining the advantages of the propensity score approach.

results.content: In a multi-period setting with time periods and multiple treatment timings (e.g., marriage or labour market entry), researchers often rely on TWFE by including individual-specific fixed effects and time-specific fixed effects , rather than group-specific indicators as in Equation 1: A Comparison of TWFE and Novel Dynamic Difference-in-Differences Estimators"):. In such settings, Goodman-Bacon, (2021) shows that the coefficient in Equation 3: A Comparison of TWFE and Novel Dynamic Difference-in-Differences Estimators") is effectively a weighted average of multiple DiD estimators, each comparing groups with different treatment timings. By contrast, if the treatment effect follows a simple step-function (a one-time increase), the outcome trajectory of the already-treated group remains parallel to the counterfactual trajectory after treatment (see Figure S1: A Comparison of TWFE and Novel Dynamic Difference-in-Differences Estimators")). At the top of Figure 2: A Comparison of TWFE and Novel Dynamic Difference-in-Differences Estimators"), we begin with the stylised example described above: trend-breaking treatment effects, two treatment timings, a sharp distinction between groups with different treatment effects, and a long panel (large ). By default, , meaning each treated unit-time pair receives its own treatment effect (similar to in Equation 4: A Comparison of TWFE and Novel Dynamic Difference-in-Differences Estimators")). Such group specific treatment effects already cause a bias in TWFE when treatment-effects are not dynamic but follow a step-level function such as in set-up 1 (see supplementary results, Figure S4: A Comparison of TWFE and Novel Dynamic Difference-in-Differences Estimators")). This highlights an important property: the sign of the bias in the TWFE summary estimate depends critically on the specific pattern of treatment effect heterogeneity over time (see supplementary Figure S5: A Comparison of TWFE and Novel Dynamic Difference-in-Differences Estimators") for an alternative fading-out pattern). Since all estimators rely on the no-anticipation assumption, they all produce biased estimates – both for the single summary treatment effect (Figure 4: A Comparison of TWFE and Novel Dynamic Difference-in-Differences Estimators"), panel 5) and for the more flexible event-time specifications (Figure 7: A Comparison of TWFE and Novel Dynamic Difference-in-Differences Estimators")). Turning to the event-time specifications (Figure 7: A Comparison of TWFE and Novel Dynamic Difference-in-Differences Estimators")), all estimators rely on at least one pre-treatment period as the reference category and implicitly assume that the treatment effect is zero in that period.
